label: CONCEPTUAL ILLUSTRATION · NO TRAFFIC CAPTURED
description: Who can see which part of one HTTPS navigation, under the stated scope. Hand-authored from protocol behaviour (RFC 8446 TLS 1.3, RFC 6066 SNI, RFC 9110 HTTP semantics, RFC 1035 DNS, WHATWG URL). No packets were captured and no TLS traffic was recorded.

example.illustrativeAddressNote: RFC 5737 documentation address used only as a label; nothing was resolved or connected.

scope: Conventional DNS query over an unencrypted transport (UDP/TCP port 53)
Trusted browser and trusted TLS-terminating server
Passive observer positioned on the path between the browser and both the DNS resolver and the TLS endpoint
These assumptions are illustrative; they are not every modern browser connection

browser.reason: The browser (or its stub resolver) forms the question for example.test.

observer.reason: Plain DNS carries the queried name without encryption.
observer.scope: Unencrypted DNS transport AND an observer between the browser and the resolver; DoH/DoT or a different vantage point changes this.

endpoint.reason: The DNS question goes to the resolver, not to the web server.
endpoint.scope: Resolver and web server are different parties.

browser.reason: The browser received the address from DNS and opens the TCP connection to it.

observer.reason: IP headers are never encrypted by TLS; routing needs them.
observer.scope: No VPN or proxy. An IP does not necessarily identify one unique website (shared hosting, CDNs).

endpoint.reason: It is the endpoint's own address; it also sees the client's source address.
endpoint.scope: Direct connection; a CDN in front would see the client address instead.

browser.reason: https: defaults to port 443 unless the URL names another.

observer.reason: TCP port numbers are in the transport header, outside TLS.

endpoint.reason: The listener accepted the connection on that port.

browser.reason: The browser sends and receives the bytes.

observer.reason: Packet times and TLS record lengths are observable even though payloads are encrypted; by themselves they do not reveal exact application content.
observer.scope: Observer on path; no padding or traffic shaping assumed.

endpoint.reason: The server sees when requests arrive and how large they are.

browser.reason: The browser writes server_name = example.test into the ClientHello.

observer.reason: The ClientHello is the first TLS message and is sent in plaintext; without ECH the server_name extension is readable.
observer.scope: No ECH. With ECH the inner ClientHello is encrypted and the outer one carries a public name.

endpoint.reason: The server uses SNI to pick a certificate and virtual host.

browser.reason: The browser decrypts the handshake with the handshake traffic keys and verifies the certificate chain.
browser.scope: TLS 1.3; the browser is a party to the key exchange.

observer.reason: In TLS 1.3 the Certificate message follows ServerHello inside the encrypted handshake; only ciphertext and record length are seen.
observer.scope: TLS 1.3 only. TLS 1.2 sent the certificate in plaintext.

endpoint.reason: It is the server's own certificate.

browser.reason: The browser builds the request line GET /account?tab=billing.

observer.reason: The request line is HTTP application data carried inside TLS records.
observer.scope: Observer is passive and does not hold the session keys.

endpoint.reason: The server decrypts and parses the request; it may log it.
endpoint.scope: The TLS-terminating party is the endpoint; if a CDN terminates TLS, the CDN sees this.

browser.reason: The browser sets Host, User-Agent, Accept and the rest.

observer.reason: Headers are inside encrypted application data.

endpoint.reason: Headers are plaintext after TLS decryption at the endpoint.

browser.reason: The browser attaches the Cookie header from its own jar.

observer.reason: The Cookie header is a header: encrypted application data.
observer.scope: Observer is passive and does not hold the session keys.

endpoint.reason: The server reads the cookie to identify the session.

browser.reason: The browser produces the body (empty for this GET).

observer.reason: Request and response bodies are encrypted application data; only their lengths and timing leak.
observer.scope: Observer is passive and does not hold the session keys.

endpoint.reason: The server receives the decrypted body.

browser.reason: #history stays in the browser's URL and is available to page JavaScript via location.hash.
browser.scope: Page JavaScript could separately read and transmit it; that would be a different request, outside this illustration.

observer.reason: The fragment is not part of the request target, so it is never serialised onto the wire.

endpoint.reason: The server never receives the fragment in the HTTP request.
endpoint.scope: Unless page JavaScript sends it in a separate request.

variants.label: Encrypted Client Hello

changes.reason: The real server_name is in the encrypted inner ClientHello; the outer ClientHello shows a public name for the ECH-fronting provider.

variants.note: ECH protects the inner ClientHello. It does not hide the destination IP, the port, timing and volume, or a plain DNS question.

variants.label: Encrypted DNS (DoH / DoT)

changes.reason: The question travels inside TLS to the resolver; an on-path observer sees a connection to the resolver, not the queried name.

variants.note: Encrypted DNS hides the question from an on-path observer. It does not hide the destination IP of the later connection, and without ECH the SNI still carries the name.

variants.label: CDN terminates TLS

changes.reason: The CDN edge is the TLS endpoint for this connection and sees the plaintext request.
The destination IP is the CDN's shared address, which may serve many unrelated sites.

variants.note: If a CDN terminates TLS it is an endpoint for that connection. Any onward connection from the CDN to the origin is a separate connection with its own visibility.

accuracy.text: Do not depict the observer reading encrypted HTTP content.
Do not depict the TLS 1.3 server certificate as plaintext on the wire.
Without ECH, SNI can reveal the requested hostname.
DNS visibility depends on transport and observer position.
Destination IP visibility does not necessarily identify one unique website.
Record lengths and traffic timing remain observable, but do not reveal exact application content by themselves.
ECH protects the inner ClientHello; it does not hide all metadata.
Encrypted DNS does not hide destination IP addresses.
If a CDN terminates TLS, it is an endpoint for that connection; any onward connection is separate.
HTTPS does not prevent phishing, compromised endpoints, or server logging.
Do not fabricate packet captures or imply actual TLS traffic was recorded.
Do not present the scope assumptions as every modern browser connection.
The hostname is used for resolution and connection setup.
The HTTP request includes the path and query.
The fragment is not included in the HTTP request target.
Page JavaScript could separately read and transmit a fragment, but that is outside the illustrated request.
